cards.text: Welcome in, friend! Psalm 117 is the shortest psalm in the whole Bible, two verses, and I've had oven TIMERS go off longer than that. But it opens BIG, with a call to praise the LORD and extol Him.

cards.question: The psalm writer opens by calling all you ___ to praise the LORD.
The psalm writer calls all the nations and peoples to praise the LORD. What reason does he give?

answers.text: His loving devotion toward us is great
He gave them all rain and harvests
He made their kings rich and strong

cards.question: In Psalm 117, the psalm writer says the faithfulness of the LORD lasts only for a season.

cards.text: He signs off with "Hallelujah!" and that's the WHOLE psalm. Then Psalm 118 opens by telling us to give thanks to the LORD, because He is good, and right behind that comes a line you're about to hear A LOT.

cards.question: Psalm 118 opens by saying the LORD's loving devotion will run out someday.

cards.text: Now he goes group by group: let Israel say, "His loving devotion endures forever." Let the house of Aaron, the family of the priests, say it too (Exodus 28:1), like a group chat where EVERYBODY has to reply with the same message before anybody can leave.

cards.question: After Israel and the house of Aaron, one more group is called to say that the LORD's loving devotion endures forever. Who is it?

cards.text: Then the psalm gets personal. The psalm writer looks back on a time he was in distress, and he called to the LORD.

cards.question: The psalm writer called to the LORD in his distress, and the LORD answered and set him ___.

cards.text: Now the psalm writer says, "The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid." Friend, I JUMP every time my own oven timer goes off, and this man is standing there calm as you please.

cards.question: Right after saying the LORD is on his side, the psalm writer asks, "What can man do to me?" What does he mean?

answers.text: With the LORD on his side people can't scare him
He is asking people for advice on what to do
He worries people have more power than God

cards.question: The psalm writer calls the LORD his helper.

cards.text: Then he compares trusting in man, even in princes, with something better. I spent years in a junk drawer trusting that the next person to open it would put me back to work, and friend... they were looking for TAPE.

cards.question: The psalm writer says one thing is better than trusting in man or even in princes. What is it?

cards.text: Now it gets tense. He says all the nations surrounded him, and then he says it again: they surrounded him on every side.

cards.question: All the nations surrounded the psalm writer. What does he say he did to them in the name of the LORD?
The psalm writer paints a picture of the nations coming at him. He says they swarmed around him like ___.

cards.text: BEES, friend! I'd be swinging this mustache around like a ceiling fan! But he says they were extinguished like burning thorns, and then he was pushed so hard he was falling.

cards.question: When he was pushed so hard he was falling, the psalm writer says he got back up on his own.

cards.text: Last stop, the psalm writer was pushed so hard he was falling, and the LORD helped him. Now he says the LORD is his strength and his song. And there's one more thing the LORD has become for him.

cards.question: The psalm writer says the LORD has become his salvation.

cards.text: Then you can hear it coming from the tents of the righteous: shouts of joy and salvation. That's the noise my bakery makes when a whole batch comes out PERFECT, except it's just me, so it's mostly me yelling at the oven.

cards.question: The tents of the righteous are shouting with joy. What do they say performs with valor?

answers.text: The right hand of the LORD

cards.text: Then the psalm writer declares, "I will not die, but I will live and proclaim what the LORD has done." And then he gets honest about the hard part too.

cards.question: The psalm writer says the LORD never disciplined him at all.

cards.text: Now he calls out, "Open to me the gates of righteousness," and he tells us why he wants in.

cards.question: The psalm writer asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened. Why does he want to go in?

answers.text: To give thanks to the LORD
To ask the priests for help
To bring news of the battle

cards.question: The psalm writer says this is the gate of the LORD, and the ___ shall enter through it.

cards.text: He thanks the LORD again for answering him and becoming his salvation. Then comes the most famous line in this whole psalm, and it's a building picture.

cards.question: In the psalm writer's building picture, what happens to the stone the builders rejected?

answers.text: It gets thrown in the river
It is left out in the field

cards.text: The stone nobody wanted becomes the CORNERSTONE, friend, and after all my years in the back of a junk drawer, that's MY kind of comeback! Jesus Himself quotes this line (Matthew 21:42), and Peter, His disciple, tells the leaders that Jesus is that stone (Acts 4:10-11).

cards.question: The psalm writer says the builders pulled off this cornerstone comeback on their own.

cards.text: He says this is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes. Then he says this is the day that the LORD has made.

cards.question: The psalm writer says this is the day that the LORD has made. What does he say we will do in it?

answers.text: Rejoice and be glad in it
Rest and be quiet in it

cards.text: Then comes a prayer for the LORD to save us and cause us to prosper, and then this: "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD." When Jesus rides into Jerusalem, the crowds shout this line about Him (Matthew 21:9).

cards.question: The psalm writer says the LORD is God, and He has made His ___ to shine upon us.

cards.text: Then comes the call to bind the festal sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar. And the psalm writer says "You are my God" TWICE, once to give Him thanks and once to exalt Him, because some things you just have to say twice.

cards.question: Psalm 118 ends with the exact same line it started with.

findings.problem: The fill in the blank asks the baker to supply the next word of Psalm 117:1 ('all you ___'). Card 1 gives no hint of who is being called, so 'nations' cannot be reasoned out over 'priests' or 'elders'. It tests wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Wrong answer 'priests' is not clearly false across the passage. Card 7 tells the baker that the house of Aaron, 'the family of the priests', is also called to declare the LORD's loving devotion (Psalm 118:3). A baker could argue that priests are among those called to praise.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: Choosing bees, locusts or flies is a pure detail guess, because all three swarm. Nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason to 'bees'. This is the same kind of card as the Psalm 23 bad example (oil, myrrh or perfume).

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The card retells Psalm 118:13 ('pushed so hard he was falling, and the LORD helped him') but cites only Psalm 118:14. This is also the first time the card set states outright that the LORD helped him.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The card opens with a recap of the last stop ('Last stop, the psalm writer was pushed so hard he was falling...') before moving forward.
'The stone nobody wanted' stretches Psalm 118:22. The text says the builders rejected it, not that nobody wanted it.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: Cards 11 and 12 already established that the builders rejected the stone, so 'the builders pulled off this cornerstone comeback on their own' is false no matter what verse 23 says. The setup rules out 'True', and the card never tests the verse's point, 'This is from the LORD'.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The story card carries three beats: the prayer to save and prosper (118:25), the 'Blessed is he who comes' line (118:26), and the Matthew 21:9 connection.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: 'Because some things you just have to say twice' gives a reason why the psalm writer repeats 'You are my God'. The text gives no reason.

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The card asks about the refrain again at its last appearance (Psalm 118:29). Stop 1 card 6 already asked about it at its first appearance (118:1).

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: No card tells several details: Psalm 118:7b ('I will look in triumph on those who hate me'), Psalm 118:18b ('He has not given me over to death'), and Psalm 118:26b ('From the house of the LORD we bless you'). Stop 2 card 6 tests only the first half of 118:18 with a False statement, so the baker never hears that the LORD did not give him over to death.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.
